title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: Before Betsy could walk out of the drawing room, she ran into Stepan Arkadyevitch in the doorway. He had just come from Yeliseev's, where a fresh consignment of oysters had arrived.
"Ah! Princess! What a delightful coincidence!" he began. "I was on my way to see you."
"A coincidence of one minute, since I'm leaving," said Betsy, smiling and pulling on her glove.
"Don't put the glove on yet, Princess; let me kiss your hand. Of all the old fashions that have come back, this is the one I'm most grateful for." He kissed Betsy's hand. "When shall we meet again?"
"You don't deserve it," Betsy answered, still smiling.
"Oh, but I do — I deserve a great deal, because I have become a very serious person. I look after not only my own business but other people's as well," he said, with a meaningful expression.

"Oh, I'm so glad to hear that!" Betsy answered, instantly understanding that he was talking about Anna. They stepped back into the drawing room and stood in a corner. "He is killing her," Betsy said in a charged whisper. "It's impossible, impossible…."
"I'm so glad you see it that way," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, shaking his head with a serious, sympathetically pained expression. "That's exactly why I've come to Petersburg."

"The whole town is talking about it," she said. "It's an impossible position. She wastes away day by day. He doesn't understand that she's one of those women who can't play games with their feelings. There are only two ways out: either he takes her away and acts decisively, or he gives her a divorce. This is suffocating her."

"Yes, yes… exactly so…." Oblonsky said, sighing. "That's what I've come for. Not only for that, of course — I've been appointed a _Kammerherr_, and naturally I have to go through the formalities of thanks. But the main thing was settling this."
"Well, may God help you!" said Betsy.

After seeing Betsy out into the front hall, kissing her hand again above the glove at the pulse, and murmuring such improper nonsense at her that she didn't know whether to laugh or be furious, Stepan Arkadyevitch went in to his sister. He found her in tears.

Though he was bubbling with cheerfulness, Stepan Arkadyevitch immediately and quite naturally fell into the sympathetic, gently emotional tone that matched her mood. He asked how she was and how she had spent the morning.
"Very, very miserably. Today and this morning, and every day that's gone and every one that's coming," she said.
"I think you're giving in to pessimism. You have to pull yourself together, you have to face life. I know it's hard, but…."

"I've heard that women love men even for their faults," Anna burst out suddenly, "but I hate him for his virtues. I can't live with him. Do you understand? Just the sight of him has a physical effect on me — it sends me out of my mind. I can't, I can't live with him. What am I to do? I used to be unhappy and thought no one could be more unhappy, but the state I'm in now is something I could never have imagined. Can you believe that, knowing he's a good man, a fine man, that I'm not worth his little finger, I still hate him? I hate him for his generosity. And there's nothing left for me except…."
She would have said death, but Stepan Arkadyevitch wouldn't let her finish.
"You're ill and worn out," he said. "Believe me, you're exaggerating terribly. There's nothing so dreadful in it."

And Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled. In his place, no one else dealing with such despair would have risked a smile — it would have looked brutal — but in his smile there was so much sweetness and almost feminine tenderness that it didn't wound; it softened and soothed. His gentle, calming words and smiles were as soothing and softening as almond oil. And Anna soon felt it.

"No, Stiva," she said, "I'm lost — lost! Worse than lost! I can't say yet that it's all over; on the contrary, I feel it isn't over. I'm an overstretched string that has to snap. But it isn't finished yet… and the ending will be terrible."
"It doesn't matter; we just have to slacken the string, little by little. There's no situation that doesn't have a way out."
"I've thought, and thought. Only one…."
Again, from her frightened eyes, he understood that the one way out she was thinking of was death, and he wouldn't let her say it.

"Not at all," he said. "Listen to me. You can't see your own situation the way I can. Let me tell you frankly what I think." Again he smiled discreetly, his almond-oil smile. "I'll start from the beginning. You married a man twenty years older than you. You married him without love, not knowing what love was. That was a mistake — let's grant it."
"A terrible mistake!" said Anna.

"But, I repeat, it's a done thing. Then you had, let's say, the misfortune of loving a man who wasn't your husband. That was a misfortune; but that, too, is a done thing. And your husband knew it and forgave it." He paused at each sentence, expecting her to object, but she said nothing. "That's how matters stand. Now the question is: can you go on living with your husband? Do you want to? Does he want to?"
"I don't know — I don't know anything."
"But you just said yourself that you can't stand him."
"No, I didn't say that. I take it back. I can't tell, I don't know anything about it."
"Yes, but let me…."
"You can't understand. I feel as though I'm falling head down into some pit, and I shouldn't try to save myself. And I can't…."
"Never mind, we'll slide something underneath and pull you out. I understand you — I understand that you can't bring yourself to put your wishes and feelings into words."
"There's nothing, nothing I want… except for it all to be over."

"But he sees that and knows it. And do you suppose it weighs on him any less than on you? You're wretched, he's wretched — and what good comes of it? Whereas a divorce would solve the whole thing." With some effort Stepan Arkadyevitch came out with his central idea, and looked at her meaningfully.

She said nothing and shook her cropped head, refusing. But from the look on her face, which suddenly brightened into its old beauty, he saw that the only reason she wasn't wanting this was that it struck her as a happiness she could never have.

"I'm terribly sorry for you! And how happy I'd be if I could fix things!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, smiling more boldly. "Don't say anything, don't say a word! May God only grant that I can speak the way I feel. I'm going to him."
Anna looked at him with dreamy, shining eyes and said nothing.
